---
title: Quickstart
description: From zero to a working GTM sandbox — the owner bootstraps with /sandbox-init, developers join with /sandbox-join, and nobody but the owner ever sees a secret value.
---

Two roles, two commands. The **owner** creates the sandbox and holds every
credential locally; each **developer** joins, runs workflows, and never sees a
single secret value.

This page assumes a plugin install with slash commands (Claude Code, ZCode — see
[Install](/docs/build/install)). In any other agent, follow the manual scaffold
path in the skill — it is the same steps done by hand.

## Owner: create a sandbox

<Steps>
### Run the bootstrap

```text
/sandbox-init ~/code/outbound-pilot
```

The command scaffolds the mono-repo — gitignored `.env.*` files, the pre-commit
guard that blocks `.env*` staging, the GitHub Actions workflow template, and
`scripts/sync-secrets.sh` — writes a minimal runner stub, and, on your
confirmation, creates the private GitHub repo and the three environments
(`development`, `pilot`, `production`). It finishes with a **names-only**
dry-run of the first secrets sync.

### Sync development secrets

```bash
scripts/sync-secrets.sh --dry-run        # what would change (key names only)
scripts/sync-secrets.sh --env development # real sync, development only
```

The script prints key names, never values. Fill `.env.pilot` and
`.env.production` when you have real credentials, and sync them the same way.

### Configure the gates

In Repo → Settings → Environments, set required reviewers:

- `pilot` — 1 required reviewer, deployment branch `main`
- `production` — 2 required reviewers, branches `main` and `v*` tags

This is what turns promotion into a human-approved hop instead of a flag flip.

### Invite the team

Invite teammates as collaborators with **write** — never admin. Point them at
`/sandbox-join`. The full owner checklist lives in
[Team access](/docs/build/team-access).
</Steps>

## Developer: join a sandbox

<Steps>
### Run the join command

```text
/sandbox-join owner/outbound-pilot
```

The command clones the repo, verifies `gh` is authenticated (no admin permission
is required or expected), and does a read-only access recon of the repo's
environments and workflows.

### Prove the chain

```bash
gh workflow run gtm-workflow.yml -f environment=development -f dry_run=true
gh run watch
```

Your dispatch injects the `development` environment's secrets into the CI job —
and only that job. You never see the values; you see the run succeed.

### Request pilot access

Paste this to the owner:

> Please add me as a required reviewer on the `pilot` environment
> (Repo → Settings → Environments → pilot), or approve my dispatches when I run
> against pilot.
</Steps>

## What a developer can and cannot do

| Capability | You now? | How to get it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Run workflows with development secrets | yes | — |
| Read or change secret values | no | never — owner-only by design |
| Run with pilot credentials | request | owner adds you as reviewer on `pilot` |
| Run with production credentials | request | owner approval on a `production` dispatch |

A task that seems to need pilot or production *values* actually needs a *run
against that environment*. If you ever need `.env.development` locally, ask the
owner to hand it over through a password manager — never chat, never git.

<Callout type="warn">
  No secret values anywhere in this flow — not in chat, tickets, code review,
  or logs. Examples use <code>replace-me</code> placeholders only. The moment a
  value exists in a transcript, treat it as public and rotate it.
</Callout>
